summary.case_overview: This writ petition, along with connected matters, challenges the constitutional validity of the Twenty-fourth, Twenty-fifth, and Twenty-ninth Amendments to the Constitution of India [Page 1] [Page 2]. The proceedings stem from challenges under Article 32 to land reform legislation in Kerala, which was subsequently placed in the Ninth Schedule by constitutional amendments [Page 1] [Page 2]. The core controversy involves determining the scope and extent of the amending power conferred by Article 368 and whether fundamental rights or basic features of the Constitution are subject to abrogation or implied limitations [Page 2] [Page 7].
summary.facts_of_case: Writ Petition No. 135 of 1970 was filed under Article 32 by His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru challenging the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, and its 1969 amendment, alleging violations of fundamental rights under Articles 25, 26, 14, 19(1)(f), and 31 [Page 1]. During the pendency of the petition, the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971 was passed, and the Constitution (Twenty-fourth, Twenty-fifth, and Twenty-ninth) Amendments were enacted [Page 1] [Page 2]. The Twenty-ninth Amendment inserted the Kerala Acts into the Ninth Schedule [Page 2]. The petitioner subsequently amended the writ petition to challenge these constitutional amendments [Page 2]. The matter was referred to a larger bench, where the correctness of the Golak Nath decision and the scope of Article 368 were examined [Page 2].
summary.legal_issues:
1. What is the extent and scope of the amending power conferred by Article 368 of the Constitution, apart from Article 13(2)? [Page 2]
2. Whether the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971 is constitutionally valid [Page 2].
3. Whether Section 2 and Section 3 of the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971 are constitutionally valid [Page 2].
4. Whether the Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972 is constitutionally valid [Page 2].
5. Whether there are any implied limitations on the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution, such as the preservation of its basic features or fundamental rights [Page 6] [Page 308].
summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners argued that the Constitution granted citizens fundamental rights intended to subsist forever and to protect them from future tyranny [Page 2]. They contended that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is limited, that fundamental rights cannot be amended out of existence, and that the basic features of the Constitution (such as secularism, democracy, and individual freedom) cannot be destroyed [Page 2] [Page 307]. Conversely, the respondents claimed that Parliament possesses plenary and limitless power under Article 368 to amend any provision of the Constitution, including fundamental rights, and that no implied limitations exist on the amending power [Page 2] [Page 32].
summary.court_reasoning: The judges delivered diverse opinions regarding the interpretation of Article 368 and the doctrine of implied limitations [Page 1] [Page 205]. Several judges reasoned that the word 'amendment' in Article 368 carries inherent or implied limitations, meaning that while provisions can be amended, the basic structure, identity, or essential features of the Constitution cannot be destroyed or abrogated from within [Page 124] [Page 144]. Other judges reasoned that Article 368 contains no express or implied limitations on the amendment of any provision of the Constitution, and that if the text is explicit and unambiguous, the Court cannot read unexpressed restrictions into it [Page 175] [Page 185].
